lead: The receiver knows the shape of the pulse that was sent but sees it buried in noise. One linear filter gives the largest possible signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant t = T: the matched filter, whose impulse response is the pulse reversed in time and delayed by T. A multiplier followed by an integrator gives the same sample and is called the correlation receiver. The best SNR it reaches is 2E/N₀, and it depends only on the pulse energy, not its shape. Modems, radar and GPS receivers are built on this.
prereq: You need: signal space (inner product and Cauchy-Schwarz), and white noise with power spectral density N₀/2 (see Foundations: signals, noise and random processes).

sections.h3: The filter that maximises the sample

blocks.text: A known pulse s(t), lasting 0 ≤ t ≤ T with energy E = ∫₀ᵀ s²(t) dt, arrives as r(t) = s(t) + w(t). The noise w(t) is white and Gaussian with two-sided power spectral density N₀/2. Pass r(t) through a filter with impulse response h(t) and sample its output at t = T. The signal part of the sample and the variance of the noise part are
ys(T) = ∫ h(τ) s(T − τ) dτ, σ² = (N₀/2) ∫ h²(τ) dτ
Here both integrals run over every τ where h(τ) is nonzero. The noise variance is the same at every sampling time, because the noise is stationary.
The output SNR is y<sub>s</sub>²(T)/σ². By Cauchy-Schwarz, [∫h(τ)s(T − τ)dτ]² ≤ ∫h²(τ)dτ · ∫s²(T − τ)dτ = ∫h²dτ · E. Dividing by σ² gives
Here E is the pulse energy in joules (across 1 Ω for a voltage pulse) and N₀ the one-sided noise density in W/Hz, so 2E/N₀ = E/(N₀/2) has no unit.

Equality needs h(τ) proportional to s(T − τ). With gain 1 that is the matched filter, h(t) = s(T − t): the pulse reversed in time, then delayed by T so that the filter is causal. In frequency, H(f) = S*(f)e−j2πfT. At t = T its signal output is E and its noise variance is (N₀/2)E, so the SNR is E²/(N₀E/2) = 2E/N₀.

For the signal alone, the output is the pulse's autocorrelation shifted to peak at t = T. For a rectangular pulse of height A this is a triangle: it rises linearly from 0 at t = 0 to A²T at t = T and falls back to 0 at t = 2T (Figure 5.5.1). Sampling early or late takes a lower point of the triangle, while the noise stays the same.

sections.h3: The correlation receiver gives the same sample

blocks.text: Multiply r(t) by a stored copy of s(t) and integrate from 0 to T:
z(T) = ∫₀ᵀ r(t) s(t) dt = E + ∫₀ᵀ w(t) s(t) dt
Here the noise term has mean 0 and variance (N₀/2)E, exactly as for the matched filter.

The multiplier, integrator and sampler form the correlation receiver (correlator); the integrator is cleared after each symbol, so it is also called integrate and dump. Put h(τ) = s(T − τ) into the matched-filter output and substitute u = T − τ: y(T) = ∫ s(T − τ) r(T − τ) dτ = ∫₀ᵀ s(u) r(u) du = z(T). The two receivers give the same number at t = T and so make the same decisions.

They differ between samples: the matched filter's output is the triangle, the correlator's is a ramp that is dumped at T. The matched filter is a fixed filter and suits hardware; the correlator is an inner product ⟨r, s⟩, which is what the signal-space picture uses. With N basis functions, a bank of N correlators gives the coordinates of r.

items: The bound 2E/N₀ depends only on E and N₀. Two pulses of equal energy give the same peak SNR, whatever their shape.
The factor 2 is real. With two-sided density N₀/2 the bound is E/(N₀/2); writing E/N₀ is 3 dB low.
The bound holds only at t = T. A mis-timed sample or a filter of the wrong shape loses SNR; the second worked example measures both losses.
The matched filter maximises SNR; it does not remove ISI. Pulse shaping and equalization are separate jobs.
It is optimum for white noise. For coloured noise, whiten the noise first, then match.

blocks.text: A mismatched filter loses SNR by the factor ρ² = ⟨hr, s⟩²/(‖hr‖²‖s‖²), where hr(t) = h(T − t) is the filter's reference shape. This is the squared correlation coefficient of the two shapes, which Cauchy-Schwarz keeps at or below 1. The comparison of this sample with a threshold, which turns SNR into an error probability, is the subject of optimum detection.

examples.question: A rectangular pulse of amplitude A = 1 V and duration T = 1 ms is received in white noise with one-sided density N₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz (take the voltage across 1 Ω). Find (a) the pulse energy, (b) the matched-filter output at t = T, (c) the maximum output SNR as a ratio and in dB.
steps: E = A²T = 1² × 1 × 10⁻³ = 1 × 10⁻³ J = 1 mJ. (V²·s across 1 Ω is W·s, that is J.)
The matched filter is h(t) = s(T − t), a 1 V rectangle on 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 ms. Its signal output at T equals E = 1 × 10⁻³ (in V²·s).
Noise variance at the output: σ² = (N₀/2)E = 1 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁻³ = 1 × 10⁻⁹.
examples.answer: E = 1 mJ, output at T is 1 × 10⁻³ V²·s, maximum SNR = 1000 = 30 dB. No other filter does better at t = T.

examples.question: For the same pulse and noise: (a) the sampler fires at 0.8T instead of T; (b) a different pulse, the ramp s(t) = At/T on 0 ≤ t ≤ T, is received with the same rectangular filter (integrate and dump) instead of its own matched filter. Find the SNR loss in each case.
steps: (a) The matched-filter output for the rectangle is the triangle y(t) = A²t for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, so y(0.8T) = 0.8E. The noise variance is unchanged at (N₀/2)E.
(b) Ramp energy E = ∫₀ᵀ (At/T)² dt = A²T/3. Integrate-and-dump output: ∫₀ᵀ (At/T) dt = AT/2; its noise variance is (N₀/2)T.
SNR = (AT/2)²/((N₀/2)T) = A²T/(2N₀). The matched filter would give 2E/N₀ = 2A²T/(3N₀).
Ratio = [A²T/(2N₀)]/[2A²T/(3N₀)] = 3/4 = 0.75, a loss of 10 log₁₀ 0.75 = −1.25 dB. This is ρ² for a ramp against a flat reference: (1/2)²/(1/3) = 0.75.
examples.answer: (a) Sampling at 0.8T costs 1.94 dB (SNR 640); (b) the flat filter on a ramp pulse costs 1.25 dB (factor 0.75).

traps: Writing the maximum SNR as E/N₀. With two-sided density N₀/2 it is 2E/N₀; E/N₀ is 3 dB low.
Using h(t) = s(t) for a pulse that is not symmetric about T/2. The matched filter is s(T − t), reversed and delayed.
Sampling the matched filter at any time other than T. For a rectangle the output at 0.8T is 0.8E and the SNR falls by 1.94 dB.
Saying the correlator and matched filter have the same output waveform. They agree only at t = T.
Claiming the matched filter removes ISI. It maximises SNR for one isolated pulse; zero ISI needs Nyquist pulse shaping or an equalizer.

quiz.q: Give the impulse response and the transfer function of the filter matched to s(t), 0 ≤ t ≤ T.
quiz.a: h(t) = s(T − t); H(f) = S*(f)e<sup>−j2πfT</sup>, where S(f) is the Fourier transform of s(t).

quiz.q: What operations make up a correlation receiver?
quiz.a: Multiply r(t) by the stored pulse s(t), integrate from 0 to T, sample at T, then clear the integrator (integrate and dump).

quiz.q: Why does the peak SNR of a matched filter depend on the pulse energy but not its shape?
quiz.a: At t = T the signal output is E and the noise variance is (N₀/2)E, so SNR = 2E/N₀. Shape changes the bandwidth and the output waveform, but not these two numbers.

quiz.q: A pulse of energy 2 mJ is received in noise with N₀ = 4 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz. Find the maximum SNR in dB.
In the first worked example the sampler fires at 0.9T. Find the output SNR in dB.
quiz.a: y(0.9T) = 0.9E, so SNR = 0.81 × 1000 = 810, which is 29.08 dB, a loss of 0.92 dB.

quiz.q: Show in one line that the matched filter and the correlator give the same sample at t = T.
quiz.a: With h(τ) = s(T − τ), y(T) = ∫h(τ)r(T − τ)dτ = ∫s(T − τ)r(T − τ)dτ; putting u = T − τ gives ∫₀ᵀ s(u)r(u)du = z(T).

quiz.q: A receiver uses h(t) = s(t) for the ramp s(t) = At/T. Is it matched? What happens at t = T?
quiz.a: No. s(T − t) is a falling ramp, while s(t) rises. The output at T is ∫s(τ)s(T − τ)dτ = A²T/6, half of E = A²T/3, with the same noise variance as the matched filter, so the SNR is 0.25 of the best: a 6 dB loss.

beyond: Radar uses the matched filter as pulse compression: a long chirp is transmitted for energy and compressed by its matched filter into a short peak for range resolution. GPS receivers correlate the incoming signal with each satellite's code, and spread-spectrum rake receivers run one correlator per multipath echo. Search for pulse compression, matched filter bound and rake receiver.

figure.caption: Top: the matched filter and the correlator give the same number at t = T. Bottom: the matched-filter output for the worked example's 1 V, 1 ms rectangle is a triangle that peaks at E = 1 × 10⁻³ V²·s at t = T; sampling at 0.8T reads only 0.8E, a 1.94 dB loss.
